title: Nothing gained (section 22)
hook: in the highest awakening, not even the least thing is gained

segments.voice: Yesterday: nothing to teach. The Buddha teaches fully, then refuses to own what he taught. Your line: no teaching, teaching. Did you hand something on without keeping a claim on it? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

So, what did you get out of it? It's a question that follows people home from all sorts of things. A weekend away. A class. A hard year. A long talk with a friend. We want to point at something we're carrying back: a skill, a lesson, a photo, a certificate. Section twenty-two of the Diamond Sutra puts that question to the Buddha's own awakening. And the answer, in the Buddha's own words, is startling. Today: nothing gained.
screen: `WHAT DID YOU GET OUT OF IT?` → `SOMETHING TO CARRY BACK.` → `ASKED OF AWAKENING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the size. Section twenty-two is only a few lines long. No sands of the Ganges, no worlds of treasure. Just a question and an answer. It reads like the moment in a long conversation when someone finally says the plain thing. Second, the question. Subhuti asks the Buddha: when you reached the highest, most complete awakening, was it that you reached nothing? He isn't being cheeky. He has been listening all through this sutra, and he's drawing the line out to its end. Third, the answer. So it is, Subhuti, so it is, the Buddha says. The words are doubled, as if to make sure nobody softens them. In that highest awakening, not even the least thing is found or gained. And that, he says, is what is called the highest, most complete awakening. The phrase in Sanskrit is anuttara samyak sambodhi: awakening with nothing above it, whole and right. The sutra's claim is that its wholeness comes from there being nothing in it to hold. Fourth, the meaning for an ordinary day. If awakening isn't a thing acquired, then it can't be stacked on a shelf with other accomplishments, or lost, or compared. One way to picture it: awakening is less like buying a lamp and more like opening the curtains. The light was never something you owned. What changes is what's no longer in the way. This doesn't make practice pointless. The Buddha practiced. The sutra keeps urging people to keep and recite it. It only means the practice isn't a purchase. You can work hard at something and still not need to walk away holding it.
screen: `A FEW PLAIN LINES.` · `WAS IT NOTHING YOU REACHED?` · `SO IT IS, SO IT IS.` · `CURTAINS, NOT A LAMP.` · then, large: `NOT THE LEAST THING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: give up one gain. Settle, and breathe. Notice what you're hoping to get out of these two minutes: calm, insight, a better mood, a streak kept. Name it quietly. Then set it down, like putting a bag on the floor beside you. Sit without needing to get anything. If the hope comes back, name it again and set it down again. Let the breath come and go, gaining nothing, losing nothing. Whatever happens in the next two minutes is enough. The bell holds the time.
Nothing gained. Section twenty-two says that in the highest awakening, not even the least thing is gained, and that is called awakening. Today's word.
Your line: not the least thing. Today, do one thing you care about without asking afterward what you got out of it. Let it be whole on its own. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: In some Zen teaching, practice is described as sitting without a gaining mind, not trying to acquire anything; section 22 is read as supporting this.

fork.setup: Subhuti asks the Buddha: when you reached the highest awakening, was it that you reached nothing? what does the Buddha say?
options: so it is, so it is
fork.reveal: he agrees, twice: not even the least thing is gained, and that is called the highest awakening.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: awakening; in anuttara samyak sambodhi, the highest, most complete awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: awakening is the biggest prize there is.
what it means: in the highest awakening not even the least thing is gained, and that is why it's called awakening.
what a scholar hears: anuttara samyak sambodhi defined by absence, and the Buddha's doubled 'so it is' confirming Subhuti's reading.
